name: Brans-Dicke Static Sphere
description: The gravitational field outside a static, spherical body in Carl Brans and Robert Dicke's theory of 1961, where a scalar field beside the metric sets the strength of gravity from place to place. With the coupling constant $\omega$ it bends light by $(3 + 2\omega)/(4 + 2\omega)$ of Einstein's value, and where Schwarzschild's horizon would stand its spheres shrink to zero area at infinite curvature, with no horizon to hide them.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The scalar field $\phi$ carries the dimensions of $1/G$, with $\phi_0$ its value far from the body, and $\omega$ is the coupling constant of Brans and Dicke's theory. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A physicist alone in an otherwise empty universe leans out of the laboratory window and fires a "22-caliber rifle" sideways, and the laboratory begins to turn [bransdicke1961]. According to general relativity a gyroscope inside keeps pointing along the path of the receding bullet and turns against the walls, so the "tiny, almost massless, very distant bullet" matters more than the "massive, nearby walls" in fixing which frames are inertial [bransdicke1961]. To Carl Brans and Robert Dicke, at Princeton in 1961, this was absolute space in Newton's sense [bransdicke1961]. Ernst Mach had argued that the inertia of a body comes from the other matter in the universe, an idea that in their words "has never found its complete expression in a physical theory" [bransdicke1961]. Their remedy puts a scalar field $\phi$ beside the metric to play the part of $1/G$, so that the masses around a place set the strength of gravity there [bransdicke1961, brans2014]. It brings one new number, the coupling constant $\omega$, and as $\omega \to \infty$ the theory becomes indistinguishable from Einstein's [will2014].¶How does such a theory treat the Sun? The theory was Brans's doctoral thesis, and for the field of a static spherical body he used isotropic coordinates and a form that Charles Misner suggested to him [bransdicke1961, brans2014]. It is $ds^2 = -h^{2/\lambda}c^2dt^2 + \left(1 + B/\rho\right)^4h^{2(\lambda - C - 1)/\lambda}\left(d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\Omega^2\right)$ with $h = (\rho - B)/(\rho + B)$ and $\lambda^2 = (C + 1)^2 - C(1 - \omega C/2)$, where $B$ sets the mass and $C$ the strength of the scalar field, $\phi = \phi_0h^{C/\lambda}$ [bransdicke1961, brans2014]. A body whose gravity is weak throughout has $C = -1/(2 + \omega)$, and at $C = 0$ the scalar field is constant and the metric is Schwarzschild's [bransdicke1961]. Brans and Dicke took the solution as valid for the Sun and went no further: the matching to a weak field, they wrote, does not "justify its use for a point mass" [bransdicke1961].¶Far from the body the theory curves space by $\gamma = (1 + \omega)/(2 + \omega)$ of Einstein's amount, so light grazing the Sun bends by $(3 + 2\omega)/(4 + 2\omega)$ of Einstein's angle and Mercury's perihelion advances at $(4 + 3\omega)/(6 + 3\omega)$ of Einstein's rate [bransdicke1961, thornewill1971]. The measured deflections were too rough to say anything about $\omega$ [bransdicke1961]. Mercury's perihelion was known to advance by $42.6 \pm 0.9$ seconds of arc a century, and on the assumption that this agrees with Einstein's value to 8 percent Brans and Dicke found $\omega \geq 6$, where their theory gives $39.4$ seconds [bransdicke1961]. Could the missing seconds be the Sun's doing? Six years later Dicke and H. Mark Goldenberg measured the Sun's shape and found its equator wider than its poles by $(5.0 \pm 0.7) \times 10^{-5}$ of the radius, a bulge that would account for 8 percent of Einstein's value for Mercury [dickegoldenberg1967]. Helioseismology now gives the Sun a quadrupole moment $J_2 = (2.2 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{-7}$, which moves the perihelion by less than a tenth of a percent of Einstein's value [will2014].¶Is the scalar field part of gravity or part of matter? Dicke's answer, in 1962, was that the choice is one of units: a transformation of the units of measure that varies from place to place puts the theory in a form where the metric satisfies Einstein's field equation and the scalar field "appears then as a 'matter field'" [dicke1962]. The two forms are now called the Jordan frame, for Pascual Jordan, whose group had worked out a theory of this type by 1955, and the Einstein frame [vanzo2012, brans2014]. In Dicke's units the metric of the static sphere is $\phi\,g_{\mu\nu}/\phi_0$, and that is the solution Iosif Fisher found in 1948 for a mass with a massless scalar field [faraoni2018, fisher1948]. The static spheres of every theory of this kind have had that form since Kirill Bronnikov's paper of 1973: Fisher's metric, in a harmonic radial coordinate, divided by $\phi$ [bronnikov1973, bronnikov1997]. A light ray is the same curve in both frames, and a falling body follows a geodesic of Brans and Dicke's metric alone, since in Dicke's units its mass changes from place to place [bransdicke1961, brans2014].¶Where Schwarzschild's horizon stands, at $\rho = B$, the spheres of Brans and Dicke's solution have zero area when $(\lambda - C - 1)/\lambda > 0$, and the curvature there is infinite [bransdicke1961, faraoni2016]. The surface that takes the horizon's place depends on $\gamma$, by a theorem of A. G. Agnese and M. La Camera from 1995: a naked singularity if $\gamma < 1$ and a wormhole if $\gamma > 1$ [agnese1995]. By 1962 Brans had three more classes of static solutions, at values of $\omega$ that make $\lambda^2$ negative, and Dicke would not connect such values with Mach's principle, so they went little noticed [brans1962, brans2014]. Written in Schwarzschild's coordinates the first class is "a power generalization of the Schwarzschild metric", $ds^2 = -A^{m+1}c^2dt^2 + A^{n-1}dr^2 + r^2A^{n}d\Omega^2$ with $A = 1 - 2r_0/r$, and in 1993 Manuela Campanelli and Carlos Lousto proposed some of its members as black holes different from Schwarzschild's [campanelli1993]. Nineteen years later Luciano Vanzo, Sergio Zerbini, and Valerio Faraoni went through those members and found wormholes and naked singularities [vanzo2012].¶The black holes of the theory are Einstein's: by Stephen Hawking's theorem of 1972 a stationary space containing a black hole solves Brans and Dicke's equations "if and only if it is a solution of the Einstein field equations" [hawking1972bd]. A star that collapses to a black hole therefore loses the "about 7%" of its measured gravitational mass that comes from the scalar interaction [hawking1972bd]. In Kip Thorne and John Dykla's account of 1971 the scalar field is radiated away during the collapse, leaving its constant value far away and a black hole of general relativity [will2014, thornedykla1971]. A star can radiate its scalar field while staying spherical, since in this theory spacetime "is dynamical even in spherical symmetry" [scheel1995]. The static sphere is one spherical vacuum of the theory among several, and J. O'Hanlon and B. O. J. Tupper exhibited others in 1972, of Friedmann's type, that change with time, so the theory has no Birkhoff theorem [ohanlon1972].

related.text: The same sphere measured in Dicke's units. Multiply Brans and Dicke's metric by $\phi/\phi_0$ and it is Fisher's, with $\gamma = (C + 2)/2\lambda$ and $b = 4B$ in Fisher's letters, a solution of Einstein's equations with a massless scalar field [dicke1962, faraoni2018].

The sphere with no scalar charge. At $C = 0$, where $\lambda = 1$, the field $\phi$ is constant and the metric is Schwarzschild's in isotropic coordinates, with its horizon at $\rho = B$ [bransdicke1961].

The weak field of a body with a number in front of every term. Far from the body Brans and Dicke's sphere sits at $\beta = 1$ and $\gamma = (1 + \omega)/(2 + \omega)$, and the Cassini spacecraft's measurement of $\gamma$ puts $\omega$ above $40{,}000$ [thornewill1971, will2014].

Gravity carried by a scalar field alone, on flat spacetime. Nordström's theory bends no light, and Brans and Dicke's keeps Einstein's metric and adds the scalar field to it [deruelle2011, bransdicke1961].

A scalar field beside the metric again, with a Maxwell field. The gravity of bosonic string theory at low energy is Brans and Dicke's with $\omega = -1$, and the dilaton is its scalar field [faraoni2016].
The general traversable wormhole. Brans and Dicke's sphere has a throat where its singularity would be when $\gamma > 1$ [agnese1995].

coordinates.convention: We use Brans and Dicke's isotropic coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi)$ and their constants $B$, $C$, and $\lambda$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ a length, and write $h = (\rho - B)/(\rho + B)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ is the rate of $ct$.
geodesics: \ddot{\rho} + \dfrac{2B\,\rho^4\,h^{(2C + 4)/\lambda}}{\lambda\left(\rho + B\right)^3\left(\rho - B\right)^3}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{2B\left(\rho\left(C + 1\right) - B\,\lambda\right)}{\lambda\,\rho\left(\rho + B\right)\left(\rho - B\right)}\dot{\rho}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(\lambda\,\rho^2 - 2B\,\rho\left(C + 1\right) + B^2\,\lambda\right)}{\lambda\left(\rho + B\right)\left(\rho - B\right)}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(\lambda\,\rho^2 - 2B\,\rho\left(C + 1\right) + B^2\,\lambda\right)\sin^2\theta}{\lambda\left(\rho + B\right)\left(\rho - B\right)}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.convention: We use Campanelli and Lousto's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, Schwarzschild's at $m = n = 0$, with $A = 1 - 2r_0/r$; in Brans's constants $r = \rho(1 + B/\rho)^2$, $r_0 = 2B$, $m = 1/\lambda - 1$, and $n = 1 - (C + 1)/\lambda$. coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, u, \theta, \phi)$, with $u$ an inverse length, Bronnikov's harmonic coordinate of the metric $(\phi/\phi_0)g_{\mu\nu}$; in Brans's constants $k = 2B$, $b = (C + 2)B/\lambda$, and $s = 2BC/\lambda$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ is the rate of $ct$.
